newsitem.title: south korea: S.Korea prepares media welcome for defector arrival.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea prepares media welcome for defector arrival.

text.p: South Korea prepared on Wednesday for the arrival of a top Pyongyang ideologue, and indicated the defector would be welcomed in the glare of publicity.
Security officials in Seoul said Hwang Jang-yop, now sheltering in the Philippines after fleeing through Beijing, would arrive in Seoul soon to end his odyssey.
They declined to give a date, but state radio said Hwang would arrive early next week.

Hwang, chief architect of North Korea's ideology of "juche", a creed of fanatic self-reliance, was flown to a hideout in the Philippines on March 18 after arriving in South Korea's consulate in Beijing on February 12.
"A transport plan has already been finalised for bringing Secretary Hwang to Seoul safely," the Korea Broadcasting System quoted a government official as saying.

Information officials on Wednesday were arranging facilities for the media, including foreign journalists, to cover the arrival of the most senior North Korean official ever to betray his communist homeland.
Foreign reporters were notified that four members of the overseas media would be allowed to witness the event.
Hwang spirited out of Beijing in secrecy and Philippine authorities have kept him under wraps, mainly for security reasons but also to try to save face for both North Korea and China.
South Korean media have reported that as part of its deal with Seoul to let Hwang leave, China insisted he must not be used for propaganda purposes.
North and South Korea are still locked in confrontation more than four decades after the 1950-53 Korean War ended. Chinese troops fought alongside North Koreans in the war.
Security officials said Hwang, ranked 24th in Pyongyang's hierarchy, planned to issue a statement on arrival in Seoul.
Meanwhile, South Korea on Wednesday was still undecided on the size of a food aid package to North Korea.

"The government will make a further contribution to help relieve food shortages in North Korea. But we have yet to decide on the size of the additional donation," said Kwon Tae-myon, a director at the Foreign Ministry.
He was speaking hours before U.S. and South Korean diplomats were due to meet North Korea's representatives in New York to hear Pyongyang's answer to an offer for peace talks.
The talks, also involving China, aim to secure a peace treaty to replace the truce that ended the Korean War.

South Korea gave $6 million and the United States $10 million to a World Food Programme appeal for $41.6 million. On Tuesday, Washington announced it would give an extra $15 million after the appeal was raised to $95.5 million.
"An announcement will be made in the near future on further food aid," said spokesman Kang Ho-yang at Seoul's National Unification Ministry.

In New York, Pyongyang was widely expected to respond favourably to peace talks but was likely to seek concessions, particularly from Washington. North Korea wants diplomatic recognition and an easing of the U.S. trade embargo.
"A serious food shortage and economic difficulties will eventually push North Korea to the peace table," South Korean Deputy National Unification Minister Lee Ho told Reuters.
